qs.q: A neonate presents with recurrent chest infections and choking on feeds, but initial routine nasogastric tube placement passed easily into the stomach without meeting resistance. Antenatal history revealed no polyhydramnios. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Pure oesophageal atresia with a long gap
Oesophageal atresia with a distal fistula
Atresia with a proximal pouch fistula
H-type tracheo-oesophageal fistula
qs.e: An H-type fistula involves an isolated tracheo-oesophageal fistula without atresia, presenting later in life with recurrent respiratory symptoms rather than immediate neonatal drooling or a blocked tube. Atresia variants always prevent standard nasogastric tube passage.
qs.s: Oesophageal Atresia and Tracheo-oesophageal Fistula: MCQs

qs.q: A pregnant woman undergoes a routine second-trimester ultrasound which reveals polyhydramnios and an absent stomach bubble. Which congenital anomaly of the fetus is most strongly suggested by this sonographic finding?
o: Congenital duodenal atresia
Congenital oesophageal atresia
Congenital tracheomalacia
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
qs.e: Inability of the fetus to swallow amniotic fluid due to oesophageal atresia leads to polyhydramnios and a small or absent stomach bubble. Duodenal atresia typically presents with a double bubble sign rather than a completely absent stomach bubble.
qs.s: Oesophageal Atresia and Tracheo-oesophageal Fistula: MCQs

qs.q: A 3-day-old term neonate presents with persistent bilious vomiting and a soft, flat abdomen since birth. The mother had polyhydramnios during pregnancy. A plain abdominal radiograph demonstrates a 'double bubble' sign with a complete absence of distal bowel gas. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism?
o: An in utero mesenteric vascular accident causing ischaemic resorption
Abnormal rotation and fixation resulting in Ladd's bands obstruction
Failure of recanalisation of the solid cord of the embryonic duodenum
Midgut volvulus with vascular compromise around the superior mesenteric artery
qs.e: Duodenal atresia is caused by the failure of recanalisation of the solid cord of the duodenum during the 8th to 10th weeks of gestation. Jejunal and ileal atresias, by contrast, are typically caused by in utero mesenteric vascular accidents.

qs.q: A 1-day-old neonate presents with non-bilious vomiting shortly after feeding, along with a maternal history of polyhydramnios. Imaging reveals a double bubble sign. The level of the obstruction is most likely located at which anatomical site?
o: At the duodenojejunal flexure near the ligament of Treitz
Proximal to the ampulla of Vater in the duodenum
Within the proximal jejunum after the ligament of Treitz
Distal to the ampulla of Vater in the second part of the duodenum
qs.e: Duodenal obstruction proximal to the ampulla of Vater typically presents with non-bilious vomiting, whereas lesions distal to the ampulla present with bilious vomiting. Both can produce a double bubble radiographic sign.
qs.s: Intestinal Malrotation and Intestinal Atresia in Children: MCQs

qs.q: A newborn presents with severe watery diarrhea from day one of life, accompanied by polyhydramnios and metabolic acidosis. Laboratory tests show hyponatremia. The condition is linked to a mutation in the SPINT2 gene. What is the diagnosis?
o: Congenital Chloride Diarrhea
Monosaccharide Malabsorption
Congenital Sodium Diarrhea
Intestinal Epithelial Dysplasia
qs.e: Congenital sodium diarrhea is an autosomal recessive disease caused by a defect in jejunal sodium/proton exchange linked to the SPINT2 gene, featuring hyponatremia and metabolic acidosis. Chloride diarrhea presents with metabolic alkalosis and high fecal chloride.

exam: What is the ultrasound criterion for polyhydramnios and why is it clinically important? — AFI >25 cm; indicates need for cause search and closer fetal monitoring.
A 28‑year‑old with gestational diabetes presents with a fundal height 5 cm above dates. What is your next step? — Order an ultrasound to measure AFI and assess fetal anatomy.
How does fetal esophageal atresia cause polyhydramnios? — Inability to swallow amniotic fluid leads to accumulation.
When would you consider therapeutic amnioreduction? — Severe symptomatic polyhydramnios (AFI >35 cm) with maternal respiratory compromise or imminent pre‑term labour.
Explain why tocolysis may be indicated in polyhydramnios‑related pre‑term labour. — Reduces uterine contractions, buying time for fetal maturation and possible amnioreduction.
Distinguish polyhydramnios from a twin pregnancy on ultrasound. — Polyhydramnios shows a single fetus with excess fluid; twins show two separate fetal hearts and sacs.
What maternal infection common in East Africa can cause polyhydramnios and how is it screened? — CMV; screen with maternal IgM/IgG serology or PCR if available.
Why is insulin preferred over oral hypoglycaemics in pregnant diabetics with polyhydramnios? — Insulin does not cross the placenta, avoiding fetal hypoglycaemia.
ai.title: Polyhydramnios
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Excessive amniotic fluid (>25 cm AFI) often signals fetal or maternal pathology. In low‑resource settings, common causes include diabetes, infections and multiple gestation. Management focuses on identifying the cause, monitoring fetal well‑being and preventing pre‑term labour.

b: AFI 5‑25 cm is normal
Deepest pocket <2 cm suggests oligohydramnios
sections.p: Polyhydramnios is an amniotic fluid index (AFI) >25 cm or a single deepest vertical pocket >8 cm on ultrasound.

b: Mild: AFI 25‑30 cm or pocket 8‑12 cm
Moderate: AFI 30‑35 cm or pocket 12‑16 cm
Severe: AFI >35 cm or pocket >16 cm
sections.p: Severity guides surveillance and delivery timing.

b: Maternal diabetes (gestational or pre‑existing)
Fetal gastrointestinal obstruction (esophageal atresia, duodenal atresia)
Fetal central nervous system anomalies (anencephaly, hydrocephalus)
Infections common in tropics (CMV, syphilis, malaria)
Multiple pregnancy or twins
Maternal anemia or high‑output states (e.g., sickle cell crisis)
Idiopathic (no cause identified)
sections.p: Group causes by maternal, fetal and placental origins; consider local disease prevalence.

b: Rapid uterine enlargement out of proportion to dates
Maternal dyspnoea or orthopnoea
Polyhydramnios‑related pre‑term contractions
sections.p: Often discovered incidentally on routine antenatal scan; later may cause maternal discomfort, dyspnoea, or pre‑term labour.

t.b: Confirms fluid volume and looks for fetal anomalies; if unavailable, use serial fundal height measurements

sections.p: Complications arise from uterine over‑distension and fetal effects.

b: Tight glycaemic control in diabetic mothers (insulin preferred, avoid sulfonylureas)
Therapeutic amnioreduction for severe symptomatic cases or when delivery is imminent
Tocolysis (e.g., nifedipine) if pre‑term contractions occur and no contraindication
Serial ultrasounds to track AFI and growth
Counselling on activity restriction and hydration
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then control fluid volume and monitor fetal status.

b: Pre‑conception diabetes screening
Prompt treatment of infections (malaria prophylaxis, syphilis therapy)
Nutrition optimisation to avoid anaemia
sections.p: Regular antenatal visits with ultrasound every 4‑6 weeks; optimise maternal health before conception.

Multiple gestation (multiple fetal hearts on Doppler)
Hydatidiform mole (snowstorm pattern on ultrasound)
sections.p: Conditions that also cause large uterine size.
